uncited: This method selects the appropriate finite difference stencil to estimate the gradient (slope) of a scalar volume field at a specific axis index, adapting to boundary conditions.
It distinguishes itself from precomputed gradient storage by computing the derivative on-the-fly and from Sobel operators by using 1D stencils rather than 3D kernels.
It serves as the core logic for the `gradientMode` selection in parent [Gradient Selection](5889-gradient-selection.md).
- The volume data $V$ is assumed to be accessible via indexing.
No explicit gradient storage structure is created by this specific selection logic; the gradient is computed and returned immediately.
Determine the stencil type based on the position of `i` relative to the boundaries `min` and `max`.
If `i` is strictly interior ($min < i < max - 1$), apply the **Central Difference** stencil.
If `i` is at or below the lower boundary ($i \le min$), apply the **Forward Difference** stencil.
If `i` is at or above the upper boundary ($i \ge max - 1$), apply the **Backward Difference** stencil.
The step size $h$ is assumed to be $1$ for discrete indices.
- **Index Bounds:** Ensure `i+1` and `i-1` do not exceed array bounds.
The logic `i <= min` and `i >= max - 1` handles the edges, but `max` must be defined as the last valid index.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ auxiliary space (no precomputed gradient grid).
- **Limitations:** Lower accuracy at boundaries ($O(h)$ vs $O(h^2)$); requires repeated computation if the same gradient is needed multiple times.
- **When to use:** When memory is constrained or when gradients are needed only at specific, sparse points.
- **When not to use:** When high accuracy at boundaries is critical or when gradients are needed densely across the volume (precomputation or Sobel may be better).
This method is derived from standard finite difference techniques for numerical differentiation.
It is a fundamental component of gradient-based volume rendering techniques, such as those used in transfer function design and shading.
